Nodes A, B, and D have an attribute x and their ids 1, 2, 4 are highlighted; node C has no x and is faded. The card maps node id to value, in storage order, for the three nodes that have it: 1 is 3, 4 is 4, 2 is 5." width="100%"} Reads one named attribute from many nodes at once and returns it as a dictionary keyed by node ID. Nodes that don't have the attribute are simply left out of the result (rather than mapped to `None`), so the dictionary can be smaller than the set of nodes queried. The graph is not modified. This is the companion of `set_node_attrs()` and is useful for: - collecting computed scores (e.g., centrality values stored by an analysis method) - checking which nodes carry a given attribute, and with what values - feeding attribute values into other methods that take `{node_id: value}` dicts, such as `rescale_node_attrs(values=...)` Keys are always integer node IDs, even when labels are passed in `nodes=`; use `get_label_from_id()` to translate them back. Dictionary order follows the graph's internal node order, not insertion order. For a tabular view of all attributes at once, use `get_node_df()`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [node_attr]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Name of the attribute to read (e.g., `"score"`, `"type"`, `"color"`). Nodes without this attribute are omitted from the result; if no node has it, an empty dict is returned. [nodes]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[int | str] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : The nodes to query, given as node IDs (`int`) or labels (`str`), which may be mixed. If `None` (the default), all nodes are queried. An unknown ID or label raises a `ValueError`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, any]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Dictionary mapping node IDs to attribute values. Only includes nodes that have the attribute set. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If a label passed in `nodes=` does not exist in the graph. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Only nodes that actually have the attribute set appear in the result. Node `C` has no `score`, so only `A` and `B` (IDs `1` and `2`) show up: ::: {#f976544f .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes( [ ("A", {"type": "user", "score": 95}), ("B", {"type": "admin", "score": 88}), ("C", {"type": "user"}), ] ) ) graph.get_node_attrs("score") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {2: 88, 1: 95} ``` ::: ::: Any attribute name works the same way, and here all three nodes have a `type`: ::: {#2cd87615 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.get_node_attrs("type") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {2: 'admin', 3: 'user', 1: 'user'} ``` ::: ::: Passing `nodes=` narrows the result down to specific nodes, which can be given as labels or IDs. The returned keys are always IDs: ::: {#6a11f46e .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.get_node_attrs("type", nodes=["A", "C"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` {1: 'user', 3: 'user'} ``` ::: ::: Converting the keys back to labels gives a more readable mapping: ::: {#92c7f4b1 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} {graph.get_label_from_id(nid): t for nid, t in graph.get_node_attrs("type").items()} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` {'B': 'admin', 'C': 'user', 'A': 'user'} ``` ::: :::
